title: Kevin Warsh Chairs His First Fed Meeting This Week. Here Is Why NRIs Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: The new Federal Reserve chairman presides over a pivotal policy decision on Wednesday as inflation climbs, rate hike odds rise, and every signal from Washington ripples through India's rupee, bond markets, and NRI investment portfolios.
body:
Kevin Warsh was sworn in as the 17th chair of the Federal Reserve less than a month ago. On Wednesday, he will preside over his first policy meeting — and the stakes could hardly be higher for the roughly five million Indian Americans navigating financial lives that span both countries.

The Federal Open Market Committee meets on June 16 and 17 with interest rates at 3.5 to 3.75 per cent, inflation running well above the Fed's 2 per cent target, and bond markets already pricing in a meaningful chance of a rate hike before year-end. The meeting itself is almost certain to produce no change. What matters is the signal: will Warsh lean hawkish, stay neutral, or try to keep the easing narrative alive?

## Why This Meeting Is Different

Every new Fed chair gets a honeymoon. Warsh's is shorter than most. He was nominated by President Trump, who has repeatedly pressured the central bank to cut rates. But the data is pushing the other way. The April consumer price index showed inflation climbing to a three-year high, driven by energy costs from the Iran-U.S. war, persistent services inflation, and tariff-driven goods price increases.

"The substance of the June meeting is less about the rate decision and more about the framing," a markets analyst at Nordea noted. The dot plot — the chart of individual Fed officials' rate projections — is expected to shift meaningfully. The rate cuts that populated the March projections are likely to disappear, replaced by a more neutral stance. Some officials may even signal a preference for hikes.

Rate futures now price a 63 per cent chance of a December rate hike, up from 48 per cent before the May jobs report. That shift has already begun to move markets.

## The Rupee Connection

For India, the Fed's stance is not academic. The rupee's trajectory is tightly linked to U.S. interest rate expectations. When the Fed signals tighter policy, the dollar strengthens, and capital flows out of emerging markets — including India.

The rupee is entering the week on a positive note, buoyed by the U.S.-Iran peace deal that sent oil prices tumbling to $83 a barrel. Traders expect it to open near 94.80 to 94.85 per dollar on Monday, its strongest level in weeks. Kotak Mahindra Bank has projected the rupee could reach 93 to 93.5 in the months ahead if oil stays low.

But a hawkish Fed could undercut that optimism. If Warsh's press conference on Wednesday signals that rate hikes are on the table, the dollar could strengthen, putting renewed pressure on the rupee and potentially reversing the gains from the Iran deal. For NRIs sending money home, the exchange rate is the single biggest variable in the value of each remittance.

## What NRIs Are Watching

The Fed's rate path touches NRI finances in at least four distinct ways.

**U.S. mortgage rates.** Indian Americans are among the most active homebuying demographics in the United States. With 30-year mortgage rates hovering near 7 per cent, any signal that the Fed will hike rather than cut rates means borrowing costs stay elevated — or climb further. For first-time buyers and those looking to refinance, Wednesday's tone could delay decisions by months.

**NRI deposit rates in India.** The RBI recently revived a 2013-style window to attract dollar deposits from non-resident Indians, offering rates not seen in a decade. Indian banks are competing aggressively for FCNR(B) deposits. But those rates are calibrated against the Fed's rate path. If U.S. rates rise, Indian banks will need to offer even higher premiums to attract NRI dollars — or risk losing out to U.S. treasuries and money market funds.

**Indian equity flows.** Foreign portfolio investors have pulled a record $30 billion out of Indian equities this year, driven by geopolitical risk and the lure of higher U.S. yields. A hawkish Fed would extend that outflow pressure. Indian IT stocks, which fell 4.2 per cent last week on AI disruption fears and hot U.S. inflation data, are particularly vulnerable. NRI investors with India-focused mutual fund portfolios are feeling the pinch.

**Bond markets.** India's benchmark 10-year bond yield has been falling, helped by the RBI's easing stance and the oil price drop. A hawkish Fed could reverse that trend by pushing U.S. treasury yields higher, which in turn forces Indian yields up and bond prices down. Indian government bonds had been attracting foreign investment — over $500 million flowed into the 5-year bond alone after the RBI's June 5 policy announcement. That momentum is at risk.

## The Warsh Uncertainty Premium

The deeper issue is that nobody quite knows what kind of Fed chair Warsh will be. During his previous stint as a Fed governor from 2006 to 2011, he was a monetary hawk who favoured higher rates. Trump nominated him expecting a dove who would cut rates on demand. The two impulses are now in direct conflict.

MarketWatch reported that Warsh may propose a comprehensive review of monetary policy strategy and communications, including re-evaluating the dot plot itself. That kind of structural change would inject uncertainty into markets for months.

"Will he emerge as the dovish figure many expected during his nomination process? Or will he embrace the more hawkish posture currently favoured by much of the committee?" one analyst asked. "The answer may determine how investors interpret monetary policy for the next several years."

For the moment, the base case is a hold-and-signal meeting. Rates stay unchanged. The dot plot shifts toward neutral. Warsh delivers a careful, consensus-seeking press conference that avoids alarming either the White House or the bond market. But even a carefully worded signal can move billions across borders.

## What to Do With This

The practical advice for NRIs is straightforward but uncomfortable: this is not a week to make big financial moves. If you are considering a large rupee transfer, the current exchange rate near 95 is already favourable by recent standards — but it could improve further if the Iran deal holds and the Fed stays neutral. Conversely, a hawkish surprise could push the rupee back toward 96 or 97.

For those with NRI deposit accounts, the RBI's FCNR(B) rates remain attractive relative to historical norms. Locking in current rates before Wednesday's meeting removes one source of uncertainty.

And for equity investors, the message from last week's market action is clear: oil-sensitive and rate-sensitive sectors will be volatile through the week. India's market rally on Friday and Monday was driven by the Iran deal. The next catalyst — positive or negative — comes from Washington on Wednesday evening.

The Fed does not make policy for India. But for the millions of Indians who hold assets, earn income, or send money across both economies, Kevin Warsh's first week in the chair may be the most consequential financial event of the summer.
